entries.title: Mayoral challenger Susana Mendoza vows to use financial acumen to tackle Chicago's $36B pension crisis
entries.summary: <p>Mayoral challenger <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/city-hall/2026/06/03/state-comptroller-susana-mendoza-mayoral-campaign-brandon-johnson-alexi-giannoulias" >Susana Mendoza</a> vowed Thursday to use the financial acumen she gained as state comptroller to rein in city spending and have the “come to Jesus” reckoning with union leaders needed to solve Chicago’s $36 billion pension crisis.</p><p>With police and fire pension funds hovering dangerously close to insolvency — assets cover just over 23% of liabilities — Mendoza said the financial wolf is at the city’s doorstep.</p><p>Stock market gains have been driven by a handful of artificial intelligence giants. If the market takes a nosedive, retirement checks that Chicago police officers, firefighters, building tradespeople and other union employees could disappear, dragging the city under, said Mendoza, who opted to not run again for state comptroller this year.</p><p>“These continuing obligations with no ability to pay them is what drags the city into bankruptcy… It’s an absolute crisis of insolvency that we are just teetering on… When the market gets a cold, we’re not going to get pneumonia here — they will go insolvent,” she said of the four city employee pension funds.</p><p>“We have to have difficult conversations that require looking at things like consolidations and things that, in the past, have been off limits. Concessions that folks might have to give so that they still have a pension… I will have the backbone to have those conversations.”</p><p>Mendoza said she would use that same fiscal discipline to erase the city’s $1 billion shortfall without relying on one-time revenues.</p><p>She condemned Mayor Brandon Johnson for borrowing <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/city-hall/2025/12/08/mayor-brandon-johnson-budget-stalemate-city-government-shutdown" >$449 million </a>to cover back pay for firefighters and police misconduct settlements, and for using a record $1 billion tax increment financing surplus to rescue Chicago Public Schools and bankroll a new teachers contract negotiated by his former boss, Chicago Teachers Union President Stacy Davis Gates.</p><p>“It’s literally stealing economic development potential out of the communities that need it most for the next 10, 20, 30 years. I will put a stop to that on Day One,” Mendoza said. “On Day One of a Mayor Mendoza administration, we’re going to rein in spending. We’re gonna stop the hemorrhaging of our finances.”</p><p>Asked whether she would consider the employee layoffs and furlough days that Johnson has ruled out, Mendoza said she would “entertain anything that needs to be done to get our fiscal house in order.”</p><p>“There are vacancies that we don’t have to fill. There are ways to do this where you can trim the budget. The mayor has not wanted to do that at all,” she said. “Why are we [spending] 40% more in a budget today than we were in 2019? COVID money was supposed to be spent one time for COVID-related expenses… We need to go back to the 2019 budget, adjust for inflation and start our negotiations there.”</p><p>The pension commission that  Johnson created shortly after taking office disbanded without releasing a single report after Gov. JB Pritzker signed a <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/city-hall/2025/08/04/jb-pritzker-police-pension-bill-brandon-johnson-pressure-chicago-budget-state-bailout" >police pension sweetener</a> that, over time, will make Chicago’s pension crisis $11 billion worse.</p><p>More recently, the Johnson administration has asked EY, the consulting firm that recommended $1.4 billion in savings and revenue-generation options for the city to consider, to devise more than a dozen strategies.</p><p>They’re likely to include pension obligation bonds and offering city employees the option of buying out a portion of their future pension benefits in exchange for a lump-sum payment. </p><p>A similar plan at the state level has reduced Illinois' pension obligations by approximately $2 billion.</p><p>Dana Levenson, who spent three years as Chicago’s chief financial officer under former Mayor Richard M. Daley, has said pension obligation bonds and deferred retirement options are “not bad ideas.”</p><p>But even if Chicago did both of those things, the pension crisis would be only marginally improved. What’s really needed, Levenson has said, is a "constitutional convention [that] discusses the state of Chicago’s pensions. That’s when you start getting into the benefits question,” he said.</p><p>Former Mayor Rahm Emanuel learned that the hard way. He spent the first of his two terms trying to negotiate pension reforms that were ultimately overturned. The state Supreme Court upheld a pension protection clause that says those benefits “shall not be impaired or diminished.”</p><p>Mendoza is well aware of those constitutional limitations. The four city funds with, as she put it, “woefully pathetic returns,” first need to be consolidated and “professionally managed,” she said.</p><p>“We’re going to have to have some real conversations that are going to be difficult” with union leaders, “but it requires that type of leadership to stabilize the rest of our budget,” Mendoza said. “If we’re driving so much of our operating expenses towards pension obligation and not getting any growth in those pensions, that compromises our ability to do anything else, including hiring police.”</p><div class="Enhancement" data-align-center> <div class="HtmlModule"><a class="AnchorLink" id="html-embed-module-0b0000" name="html-embed-module-0b0000"></a><iframe allow="monetization" frameborder="0" height="200" scrolling="no" src="https://play.prx.org/e?ge=prx_12963_25aa6c52-3a72-4ed9-905c-2cca83ede8fb&uf=https%3A%2F%2Fpublicfeeds.net%2Ff%2F12963%2Ffeed-rss.xml" style="min-width: 300px;" width="100%"> </iframe> </div> </div><p></p>

entries.title: Más de 170,000 están aún sin energía mientras el área de Chicago se prepara para más posibles tormentas
entries.summary: <p>Apagones generalizados, interrupciones en el servicio de trenes, cancelaciones de vuelos y árboles caídos afectaron el área de Chicago la mañana del jueves, mientras se aproxima otro sistema de clima potencialmente severo.</p><p>La tarde del miércoles cayó cerca de una pulgada de lluvia en toda el área de Chicago, con vientos que alcanzaron más de 70 millas por hora, según el Servicio Nacional de Meteorología (NWS). La posibilidad de un clima más severo el jueves aumenta el riesgo de inundaciones repentinas.</p><p>"Ya hemos tenido al menos algunos problemas menores de inundación y acumulación de agua en gran parte de la zona metropolitana desde anoche", dijo Kevin Doom, meteorólogo de NWS. "Aunque gran parte de eso ya se ha retirado, todavía hay agua en el suelo... así que el área es, en esencia, un poco más susceptible a inundaciones".</p><div class="RichTextSidebarModule Enhancement" data-module data-align-center><a class="AnchorLink" id="module-920000" name="module-920000"></a> <div class="RichTextModule-items RichTextBody"><h3>La Voz Chicago WhatsApp</h3>Encuentra más noticias en nuestro canal de WhatsApp. <a class="Link" href="https://www.whatsapp.com/channel/0029Vb0XT1XCHDylm3rCs40P" target="_blank" ><b>Síguenos.</b></a></div> </div><p>Las tormentas del miércoles fueron causadas por un "gran y prolífico sistema de tormentas" sobre el sur y el centro de Canadá, que se desplaza hacia el Medio Oeste, según el servicio meteorológico. El sistema ha estado soplando aire húmedo hacia la región, lo que favorece tormentas eléctricas severas el jueves.</p><p>"Hoy hará mucho calor y mucha humedad, muy parecido a ayer", dijo Doom. "Es un patrón cíclico de un ambiente propicio para el clima severo".</p><p>No había advertencias ni avisos en vigor a primera hora de la mañana del jueves, pero Doom anticipa lluvias de un sistema que se mueve hacia el este a través de Iowa temprano en la tarde, antes de que se aproxime el "espectáculo principal" en algún momento entre las 6 p.m. y las 8 p.m.</p><div class="Enhancement" si apuntarán a un área en particular", dijo Doom. "Pero diré que el ambiente en general en realidad parece un poco mejor para el clima severo de lo que era ayer".</p><p>El impacto de las tormentas del miércoles aún se sentía en toda el área de Chicago. Más de 172,000 clientes de ComEd permanecían sin electricidad hasta las 8:50 a.m. el jueves, según el <a class="Link" href="https://www.comed.com/outages/experiencing-an-outage/outage-map" target="_blank" >mapa de cortes de energía</a> de la agencia.</p><p>En el Aeropuerto Internacional O'Hare, al menos 54 vuelos fueron cancelados, mientras que otros 130 fueron retrasados a las 9 a.m., según <a class="Link" href="https://www.flightaware.com/live/cancelled/today/ORD" target="_blank" >FlightAware</a>. En Midway, al menos 37 vuelos estaban retrasados.</p><p>En tierra, los trenes de la Línea Amarilla de la Autoridad de Tránsito de Chicago (CTA) volvieron a circular después de que el servicio se detuvo durante aproximadamente dos horas la mañana del jueves, cuando una rama de árbol cayó sobre las vías cerca de la estación Oakton en Skokie tras la fuerte tormenta y el viento que recorrieron la zona durante la noche.</p><p>La suspensión del servicio fue anunciada alrededor de las 5:40 a.m., y los trenes seguían operando con retrasos residuales alrededor de las 7:50 a.m., según una alerta de Bridgeview.</p><p>"Nuestra prioridad es garantizar la seguridad de los litigantes, abogados, empleados de la corte y miembros del público, al tiempo que mantenemos el acceso a los servicios judiciales esenciales”, dijo el juez principal Charles S. Beach II en un comunicado que anunciaba el cierre. “La corte ha tomado medidas para asegurar que los asuntos de emergencia, incluyendo las comparecencias iniciales en casos penales y las peticiones de órdenes de protección, continúen siendo escuchados sin interrupción durante este cierre temporal”.</p><p>Además, las ramas 35 y 38 de la Corte de Circuito del Condado de Cook también se vieron afectadas por un corte de energía relacionado con el clima en su edificio ubicado en 727 E. 111th St., y todos los casos programados para el jueves ahora se escucharán el 25 de junio, según un comunicado de prensa de la Oficina del Juez Principal.</p><p>Doom insta a los residentes y viajeros a estar al tanto del pronóstico en sus áreas y actuar de manera proactiva moviendo vehículos a sus garajes o llevando objetos sueltos adentro.</p><p>"Realmente queremos que la gente solo esté atenta y se cuide a sí misma y observe cómo están evolucionando las cosas aquí más tarde esta tarde", dijo Doom.</p><p><i>Traducido con una herramienta de inteligencia artificial (AI) y editado por </i><a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/la-voz" target="_blank" ><i>La Voz Chicago</i></a></p>

entries.title: Bears to wear 'Rivalries' uniform on Christmas Day vs. Packers
entries.summary: <p>The <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/bears" target="_blank" >Bears</a> will wear their “Rivalries” alternate uniform set one time this season: on Christmas Day against the Packers at Soldier Field.</p><p>The team announced the decision Thursday when they listed the theme games for each contest this season.</p><p>The NFC North is one of two divisions, along with the AFC South, that will wear Nike’s “Rivalry” uniform this season. The teams are expected to unveil what they look like in August. The AFC East and NFC West wore them last year.</p><p>The uniform designs are meant to “ celebrate the traditions, communities and competitive spirit” of each team. entries.title: Critican administración de Trump por el trato a los que ingresan al Mundial de otros países
entries.summary: <p>Grupos de derechos de inmigrantes en Chicago están criticando el trato que la administración de Trump está dando a los oficiales y jugadores de la Copa Mundial de la FIFA mientras ingresan a Estados Unidos esta semana para el torneo de fútbol que se efectúa cada cuatro años</p><p>Aproximadamente tres cuartos de los partidos de la Copa Mundial se jugarán en Estados Unidos, con algunos partidos adicionales en México y Canadá del 11 de junio al 19 de julio. Chicago no albergará ningún partido, pero se programó un partido de exhibición entre Irak y Venezuela la noche del martes en Bridgeview.</p><p>Muhammad Sankari, director organizador de la Red de Acción Árabe Estadounidense en Chicago, dijo que las acciones contra jugadores, oficiales y aficionados de la Copa Mundial que ingresan a Estados Unidos han llevado a las organizaciones locales a prepararse para un aumento de la presencia del Servicio de Inmigración y Control de Aduanas (ICE) en los estadios anfitriones y las fiestas para ver el partido.</p><div class="RichTextSidebarModule Enhancement" data-module data-align-center><a class="AnchorLink" id="module-550000" name="module-550000"></a> <div class="RichTextModule-items RichTextBody"><h3>La Voz Chicago WhatsApp</h3>Encuentra más noticias en nuestro canal de WhatsApp. <a class="Link" href="https://www.whatsapp.com/channel/0029Vb0XT1XCHDylm3rCs40P" target="_blank" ><b>Síguenos.</b></a></div> </div><p>"La realidad es que miles y miles de personas en el área de Chicago están emocionadas por ver la Copa Mundial, y esta administración, con su racismo y su continua persecución de las comunidades inmigrantes y comunidades en todo Estados Unidos, pone en riesgo la capacidad de nuestra comunidad de reunirse, de unirse y ver uno de los eventos deportivos más importantes que sucede cada cuatro años", dijo Sankari en una </div> </div><p>A varios miembros de la selección nacional de Irán se les negó la visa por parte de Estados Unidos, y el equipo recientemente tuvo que trasladar su base de entrenamiento de Arizona a Tijuana, México. La capacidad del equipo para ingresar a Estados Unidos ahora se limita a cruzar la frontera para cada uno de sus partidos en Los Ángeles y Seattle y se requiere que el equipo abandone el país inmediatamente después de cada uno de esos partidos.</p><p>Un portavoz de DHS negó que el equipo iraní tuviera que viajar de ida y vuelta en el mismo día.</p><p>"Gracias a la generosidad del presidente Trump, el equipo iraní podrá llegar el día antes de sus partidos", dijo el portavoz del DHS en un comunicado. El portavoz no proporcionó más comentarios.</p><p>La selección nacional de Senegal fue detenida e inspeccionada el domingo en la pista del aeropuerto de San Antonio, Texas. Los miembros de la selección nacional de Uzbekistán también fueron sometidos a controles de seguridad adicionales, según informes de noticias.</p><p>FIFA no respondió de inmediato a una solicitud de comentario.</p><p>Las restricciones se producen meses después de que <a class="Link" href="https://www.congress.gov/crs-product/IN12631" target="_blank" >la administración de Trump impusiera una prohibición de viaje</a> sobre países mayoritariamente africanos y del Medio Oriente.</p><p>Los defensores de inmigrantes solicitaron a la administración de Trump que levantara todas las prohibiciones de viaje y detuviera cualquier restricción de viaje contra los oficiales de la Copa Mundial.</p><p>"La Copa Mundial debería ser un momento que una a las personas a través de fronteras, culturas y continentes", dijo Fasika Alem, directora de programas de la Organización Africana Unidas. "No debería usarse para reforzar la exclusión. Si Estados Unidos va a albergar al mundo, debe darle la bienvenida al mundo".</p><p>La Coalición por los Derechos de Inmigrantes y Refugiados de Illinois (ICIRR) organizará una fiesta para ver la Copa Mundial “libre de ICE” el sábado en la Pequeña Palestina en Bridgeview. La organización contará con personal de respuesta rápida en la fiesta, que será sólo por invitación, y negará la entrada a los agentes de inmigración si se presentan sin órdenes firmadas, dijeron los organizadores.</p><p><i>Traducido con una herramienta de inteligencia artificial (AI) y editado por </i><a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/la-voz" target="_blank" ><i>La Voz Chicago</i></a></p>

entries.title: Mexico opens 2026 World Cup with a 2-0 win over South Africa
entries.summary: <p>MEXICO CITY — Julián Quiñones and Raúl Jiménez helped Mexico make an exuberant start to the World Cup on Thursday, scoring a goal each in a 2-0 win over South Africa in the opening match of the tournament.</p><p>With a capacity crowd of 80,824 watching at Azteca Stadium, co-host Mexico started the largest World Cup tournament in history by getting goals in each half while three red cards were shown — two for South Africa and one for Mexico.</p><p>Quiñones, who was the top scorer in the Saudi league this season, gave Mexico the lead in the ninth minute. Jiménez added the second goal on a header in the 66th.</p><p>South Africa players Sphephelo Sithole and Themba Zwane were both given red cards, forcing the team to finish the match with only nine players. Mexico defender César Montes was then given a red card in injury time.</p><p>With his 46th international goal, and his first in three World Cups, Jiménez tied Jared Borgetti for second place for the Mexican national team. He is six goals shy of leader Javier "Chicharito" Hernández.</p><p>Quiñones, a 29-year-old forward who was born in Colombia, was one of six starting players who made their World Cup debut for El Tri.</p><p>Mexico, coming off a first-round exit at the 2022 World Cup in Qatar, has three points in Group A and will next play South Korea next Thursday in Guadalajara.</p><p>South Africa will play the Czech Republic on the same day in Atlanta.</p><p>This year's World Cup has 48 teams, the most in history. It is being held in Mexico, Canada and the United States.<br></p>

entries.title: MAGA YouTube star who spurred federal crackdown in Minneapolis to speak at Illinois GOP gala
entries.summary: <p>YouTube creator Nick Shirley has filmed himself interviewing Alex Jones outside the U.S. Capitol on Jan. 6, called street vendors in New York City "dangerous migrant scammers" and described a "Somali takeover" in Minnesota.</p><p>Shirley was also granted permission to accompany ICE agents during arrests in Chicago last year.</p><p>On Friday, Illinois Republicans will feature the far right influencer as a keynote speaker at their "Red Gala" fundraiser in Elk Grove Village. </p><p>The Illinois Democratic Party is calling Shirley's inclusion proof that the Illinois Republican Party "has completed their transformation into an extremist MAGA organization that values bigoted culture wars over the issues their voters care about most." State Republicans, on the other hand, are praising the 24-year-old YouTube star as "one of the fastest rising independent journalists in America, known for going where mainstream media won't."</p><p>Republican gubernatorial candidate Darren Bailey has also shown support for Shirley, writing on social media in April that Illinois should "deploy a brigade of Nick Shirleys to root out fraud in Medicaid, unemployment, and every pork barrel slush fund."</p><p>Shirley is best known for capturing the attention of the Trump administration in December when he posted a 43-minute video in which he claimed to have uncovered $110 million in fraud at Somali-run day care centers in Minnesota. In some instances, Shirley declared there was fraud because he didn't see any children, despite some of the sites appearing to be closed. The Minnesota Star Tribune visited the 10 facilities featured in Shirley's video, and found children inside four of them when invited inside. Six other facilities were either closed or employees didn't let them in. </p><p>Within two weeks of that video going viral, the Trump administration sent thousands of federal agents to Minnesota to crack down on illegal immigration — and also announced an effort to combat "the Somali-dominated scams that have bled taxpayers dry." The administration also froze funding for child care subsidies in five Democratic states, and Minnesota Gov. Tim Walz suspended his reelection, which Shirley took credit for. The CEO of Future Leaders Early Learning, a center featured in his video, was charged last month with wire fraud and conspiracy with for allegedly stealing over $4.6 million through false claims to federal nutrition and state childcare assistance programs.</p><p>While fraud investigations were already underway for years in Minnesota, Shirley was credited by the GOP for amplifying the problem — despite holes in his viral video.</p><p>The Illinois Republican Party has struggled to raise funds after the high profile departures of former Gov. Bruce Rauner and Ken Griffin — billionaires who both now live in Florida. They also have little political power in the blue state of Illinois, where they hold just three congressional seats out of the state's 19-member federal legislative delegation. The party also replaced their chair Kathy Salvi last month — less than two years after she was elected to the post. Bob Grogan, a former DuPage County auditor who also serves as a Certified Fraud Examiner, is now leading the party. </p><p>The Illinois Democratic Party lambasted the Illinois GOP, including party leaders, elected officials and candidates for office, for inviting Shirley and "lending credibility to an individual who spreads dangerous and hateful misinformation."</p><p>“Nick Shirley’s aim is to contaminate our politics with racism, xenophobia, and lies," a spokesperson said. "By welcoming him to their event, the [Illinois GOP] is revealing just how extreme they’ve become. Illinois voters can see clearly that the party has abandoned working families in favor of serving Donald Trump and his MAGA allies.”</p><p>Grogan on Thursday responded to criticisms of Shirley, telling the Sun-Times "JB Pritzker and Illinois Democrats are terrified of Nick Shirley coming to Illinois after he exposed billions of dollars in fraud in Minnesota and California."</p><p>"Illinois is next," Grogan said.</p>

entries.title: Nurses at St. Mary Hospital in Chicago go on one-day strike
entries.summary: <p>Standing in the middle of the picket line early Thursday outside St. Mary of Nazareth Hospital, Jesus Hernandez felt as if the one-day strike was already a success just an hour after it started.</p><p>Hernandez was among six nurses who <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/health/2026/06/03/fired-nurses-voice-concerns-over-working-conditions-st-mary-of-nazareth-hospital-amidst-push-to-unionize-chicago" target="_blank" ><u>were fired</u></a> in recent weeks just as nurses in the Ukrainian Village hospital prepared to hold an election to unionize with the National Nurses Organizing Committee/National Nurses United. In a sea of blue and red, Hernandez saw nurses he didn’t know well who joined the picket line to support them.</p><p>“I am not scared, I’m not backing down,” Hernandez said. “I’m still here in the fight because what we’re doing here is important, because companies don’t care about patients, they don’t care about staff. We care about patients because we deal with them day in and day out.”</p><p>Motorists along Division Street honked at the lively crowd that included about 200 nurses holding signs saying, “You can’t fire solidarity,” and, “On strike for my patients.” Security guards stood outside the hospital’s main entrance and parking lots, but the strike continued without incident. It is expected to end at 7 a.m. on Friday.</p><p>The strike comes less than a week before about 400 St. Mary’s nurses plan to vote on June 17 on forming a union. During the rally, union representatives and nurses called on the hospital to reinstate the six terminated nurses. Prime Healthcare, a large national for-profit hospital network, acquired St. Mary’s and several other Chicago-area hospitals last year.</p><p>“We’re done with Prime cutting positions, like admissions nursing, who help our patients get settled and give us time to take care of all our patients,” said nurse Daisey Moreno. “Prime is more focused on cutting staff and firing nurses than taking care of our patients. … It’s time to reinstate our co-workers and get ready to bargain.”</p><div class="Enhancement" data-align-center> <div class="Enhancement-item"> <bsp-carousel class="Carousel private employers, including hospitals, to penalize workers for forming a union, according to the National Labor Relations Board, an independent federal agency that protects the right to organize.</p><p>It was the second rally this week in support of nurses unionizing at Chicago-area hospitals, part of a larger wave of labor action in health care across the country. At both rallies, nurses called for hospitals to reinstate their co-workers who were fired just as they were forming unions with separate labor groups.</p><p>A chorus of Democratic elected officials have joined the fight to support nurses across the region, from Illinois Secretary of State Alexi Giannoulias and U.S. Sen. Bernie Sanders, to State Sen. Celina Villanueva.</p><p>St. Mary Hospital and its owner Prime would not say how many nurses worked Thursday, saying only in a statement that it was, “fully staffed as planned to meet the needs of our patients and deliver safe, high-quality care.”</p><p>“We respect the right of our employees to engage in lawful, protected, union activity, and we remain committed to ongoing, good-faith discussions with our nurses,” the hospital said.</p><p>Noemi Malave and her 17-year-daughter, Crystal Gonzales, walked past the picket line after physical therapy at the hospital. They said the hospital appeared normal except for the heightened presence of security guards. They were told to wear visitor badges, which they usually don’t have to do.</p><p>Malave, of Logan Square, said her grandmother died at the hospital and her mother was a cancer patient there. Although nurses say the hospital has changed under new management, Malave said she hasn’t noticed anything different in the quality of care in recent years.</p><p>“The nurses work very hard and many at different hours,” Malave said. “...I think they deserve whatever they’re asking for.”</p><p>But Moreno, the nurse, told the crowd during the strike rally that she noticed Prime cut corners to save money, including getting rid of a charity fund that helped patients purchase medications.</p><p>“I want every one of my patients to get everything they need to get better,” Moreno said. “My job as a nurse is to take care of them and to advocate for them, and that’s why I wanted to be part of forming our union.”</p><p>Nancy Delgado was among those who were recently fired from St. Mary after working as a nurse for seven years. The single mother worries about the savings she’s had to rely on since she lost her job, but she also wants to set an example for her daughter by speaking up.</p><p>“I want to show my daughter that our voices matter, no matter where you are, who you are,” Delgado said. “You have the right to raise your voice and to speak up the truth, especially if you work in health care.”</p><p>The escalated union action at St. Mary’s is part of a larger wave of <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/health/2026/05/18/rush-nurses-unionize-celebrate-vote" target="_blank" ><u>unionization among Chicago-area nurses. </u></a></p><p>On Wednesday, dozens of people — elected officials, nurses and Teamsters representatives — rallied at Endeavor Health’s corporate headquarters in Evanston to The sign refers to Endeavor CEO Gerald “J.P.” Gallagher.</p></figcaption><span class="line"></span><div class="Figure-credit"><p>Kristen Schorsch/WBEZ</p></div></div> </figure> </div> </div><p>Endeavor is a nonprofit and one of the biggest hospital systems in the Chicago area, treating more than 1 million patients a year and employing more than 27,000 people, according to the health system. It generated about $6.4 billion in revenue in 2025, its most recent <a class="Link" href="https://emma.msrb.org/P22033749-P21548425-P22006587.pdf" target="_blank" ><u>annual financial statement</u></a> shows.</p><p>Endeavor nurses implored their hospitals to respect the nurses’ right to unionize, to stop surveilling and intimidating them, and to reinstate <a class="Link" href="https://www.wbez.org/health-medicine/2026/06/03/u-s-congressman-endeavor-health-stop-retaliating-against-unionizing-nurses" target="_blank" ><u>two nurses at Endeavor’s Evanston Hospital who were fired</u></a>, allegedly over unionizing efforts.</p><p>Nurses are organizing over pay cuts and what they say is dangerous understaffing that could harm patients.</p><p>“Nurses are working in conditions that put their license at risk, but more importantly, the lives of the people we care for are at risk,” said Stacey Oswald, a critical care nurse at Endeavor. “Management has unrealistic, penny-pinching expectations that stretch us too thin and leave our units unsafely staffed.”</p><p>She underscored how Endeavor managers have received bonuses while cutting pay for nurses amounting to thousands of dollars a year. Records show Endeavor CEO Gerald Gallagher <a class="Link" href="https://app.candid.org/profile/14586470/endeavor-health-87-4520691?activeTab=7" target="_blank" ><u>made just over $5 million</u></a> in 2024, including a $1.4 million bonus, as well as retirement and other “deferred” compensation, Endeavor’s most recent tax return shows. That same year, the health system had a $494 million operating loss, much of it from <a class="Link" href="https://www.chicagotribune.com/2025/02/19/endeavor-health-fabio-ortega-settlements/" target="_blank" ><u>legal settlements</u></a>, <a class="Link" href="https://emma.msrb.org/P11844429-P11412902-P11855647.pdf" target="_blank" ><u>an audited financial statement</u></a> shows.</p><p>A spokesperson with Endeavor shared a previous statement. They say they respect the nurses’ right to organize, but they must prioritize patient safety.</p><p><i>Elvia Malagón covers health care for the Sun-Times. Kristen Schorsch covers health care for WBEZ.</i></p><div class="RelatedList Enhancement" data-module data-align-center> <div class="RelatedList-title">Related</div> <ul class="RelatedList-items"> <li class="RelatedList-items-item"> <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/health/2026/06/03/fired-nurses-voice-concerns-over-working-conditions-st-mary-of-nazareth-hospital-amidst-push-to-unionize-chicago" >Fired nurses allege retaliation for voicing concerns about conditions at St. Mary of Nazareth Hospital</a> </li> <li class="RelatedList-items-item"> <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/health/2026/06/03/u-s-congressman-endeavor-health-stop-retaliating-against-unionizing-nurses" >Congressman tells Endeavor Health to stop retaliating against unionizing nurses</a> </li> </ul> </div> <p></p>

entries.title: Phil Mickelson expelled from private golf club for inappropriate contact with female employee: report
entries.summary: <p>Phil Mickelson has been kicked out of a San Diego golf club over allegations he made unwanted physical contact with a female employee, Golf Digest reported Thursday.</p><p>Golf Digest cited multiple sources as saying Mickelson is no longer welcome at The Farms Golf Club in Rancho Santa Fe, California, where the six-time major champion has played and practiced for decades. The unwanted contact was said to have happened earlier this spring.</p><p>Mickelson, the chief recruiter in the launching of LIV Golf, has only played once this year because of a serious family health matter that has not been disclosed. He did not play the Masters and PGA Championship, and is no longer exempt for the U.S. Open.</p><p>Golf Digest said it verified the identity of The Farms employee and was withholding her name to protect her privacy. It said she declined to participate in the reporting of the story.</p><p>A spokesperson for Mickelson told Golf Digest, "Any misunderstanding has been cleared up. Phil continues to attend to a family health matter and is uncertain when he will be able to return to professional golf."</p><p>Golf Digest cited sources in reporting Mickelson approached the woman in the clubhouse and made nonconsensual and inappropriate physical contact with her. The woman rejected his advances and reported it to her supervisors.</p><p>Officials at The Farms reviewed and investigated, Golf Digest reported, and then confronted Mickelson on the course. Mickelson, 55, was told to leave the premises.</p><p>The Farms said in a statement to Golf Digest, "Following a staff member report of member misconduct, the club provided immediate and ongoing support to the staff member, conducted a thorough independent investigation of the incident and took decisive action. This individual is no longer a member of The Farms Golf Club."</p><p>"To protect the safety and privacy of our staff and member, we are unable to speak further on the matter."</p><p>Golf Digest cited multiple sources in confirming the member was Mickelson.</p><p>The Farms, located about 10 miles from Torrey Pines, is a private club where several top players are members such as Annika Sorenstam and Xander Schauffele, both of whom have primary residences in Florida.</p><p>The development adds to what has become a dark chapter for Mickelson, who is married with three children and was once one of the most beloved public figures in golf for his bold and creative game, and for the time he spent after rounds signing autographs.</p><p>Mickelson was a relief defendant in an insider trading scheme in 2016 in which he was not criminally charged but agreed to repay nearly $1 million he made in a single trade. Noted gambler Billy Walters was involved in that case and sentenced to five years in prison.</p><p>Walters wrote an autobiography in 2023 in which he claims Mickelson has wagered more than $1 billion over the last 30 years, including one day in 2011 in which Mickelson was said to have placed 43 bets on Major League Baseball that resulted in $143,500 in losses.</p><p>Mickelson became the oldest major champion in golf history when he won the 2021 PGA Championship. A year later, he was a central figure in helping to launch Saudi-funded LIV Golf. He lost major sponsorships when he was quoted in early 2022 as calling the Saudis "scary mother (expletives)" and that he was only thinking of joining the league to gain leverage over the PGA Tour.</p><p>The Public Investment Fund of Saudi Arabia is ending its financial support of LIV after this year.<br></p>

entries.title: Héctor Lozano habla de sus comienzos y está listo para liderar la cobertura de la Copa Mundial de Telemundo
entries.summary: <p>En la secundaria, Héctor Lozano era un destacado jugador de fútbol como lateral izquierdo en la Farragut Career Academy. También jugaba en un equipo de club, Atlas, que grababa sus partidos en una videocámara. Los jugadores se reunían en alguna casa, pedían pizza y volvían a ver cada uno de los partidos.</p><p>Lozano se lastimó el tobillo en uno de esos partidos y quedó fuera del juego. El hombre que sostenía la videocámara le dijo a Lozano que él tenía un micrófono y le sugirió que hiciera los comentarios mientras se recuperaba.</p><p>“Yo pensé, ‘¿Por qué no?’”, le dijo Lozano al Sun-Times. “Luego, después del partido, comenzamos a hacer entrevistas con mis compañeros y realmente nos divertimos. Solo hablando tonterías sobre mis amigos frente a la cámara. Lo hacíamos muy divertido.”</p><div class="RichTextSidebarModule Enhancement" data-module data-align-center><a class="AnchorLink" id="module-c30000" name="module-c30000"></a> <div class="RichTextModule-items RichTextBody"><h3>La Voz Chicago WhatsApp</h3>Encuentra más noticias en nuestro canal de WhatsApp. <a class="Link" href="https://www.whatsapp.com/channel/0029Vb0XT1XCHDylm3rCs40P" target="_blank" ><b>Síguenos.</b></a></div> </div><p>Eventualmente, Farragut comenzó a ofrecer una clase de producción de televisión y Lozano se inscribió.</p><p>“Fue como si se encendiera un foco”, dijo.</p><p>Hoy, Lozano, de 58 años, es el ancla de deportes activo con más tiempo en Chicago, en su año 31.</p><p>Desde 2021, ha aparecido en el “Noticiero Telemundo Chicago”, y esta semana comenzó a liderar la cobertura de la Copa del Mundo de la estación. Telemundo, parte de NBCUniversal, es el hogar exclusivo en español de cada partido.</p><p>“No me he perdido un partido de la Copa del Mundo en más de 30 años”, contó Lozano. “Es la Copa del Mundo más grande de la historia: 104 partidos, 48 equipos. Mucho más que cubrir y va a estar ocupado. Las primeras dos semanas de la fase de grupos habrá tres, cuatro partidos al día”.</p><p>¿Cómo puede verlos todos?</p><p>“No lo sé”, agregó, “pero voy a hacer un esfuerzo.”</p><p>La historia de Lozano es la de miles de inmigrantes que llegaron a Estados Unidos en busca de una vida mejor. Nació en León, Guanajuato, México, en una familia de 10, con tres hermanos y cuatro hermanas. Su padre, Juan, fue el primero en llegar a Estados Unidos. Héctor llegó cuando tenía 11 años.</p><p>La familia vivió primero en Pilsen y luego en La Villita. Lozano puede nombrar la intersección cercana a cada casa: Cermak y California, Cermak y Wood, 22nd y California, 30th y Christiana. La primera casa tenía un piso y un ático, que Juan convirtió en el espacio de vida de los muchachos.</p><p>“No teníamos todo”. dijo Lozano, “pero nunca nos faltó nada”.</p><p>Juan trabajaba como igualador de colores en la fábrica de Color Communications Inc., produciendo muestras. Le inculcó a Héctor su amor por el fútbol, llevándolo a él y a sus hermanos al Douglass Park los fines de semana. Más adelante, Héctor se unió a su padre en la fábrica mientras asistía al Columbia College, donde estudió radiodifusión.</p><p>“Realmente me gustaba el trabajo, pero no pagaba mucho”, dijo Lozano. “Y tenía otras aspiraciones”.</p><p>Lozano comenzó su carrera en radiodifusión en la radio WIND, que en ese momento era en español. Después de que la estación obtuvo los derechos de transmisión de un partido internacional de fútbol en Soldier Field, la gerencia se dio cuenta de que no tenía a nadie que pudiera hacer comentarios. Lozano, que era un empleado de medio tiempo, levantó la mano.</p><p>No importaba que no lo hubiera hecho desde la secundaria. Mantuvo eso en secreto. Lo único que la estación necesitaba saber era que Lozano había comentado un partido de fútbol antes, y lo hizo con entusiasmo.</p><p>Eso llevó a más oportunidades, entre ellas comentar las temporadas 1992-93 y 1993-94 de los Bulls junto a Héctor Molina. Lozano estuvo al micrófono para el tiro de John Paxson que ganó las Finales de la NBA en 1993 y para el infame llamado de falta de Hue Hollins sobre Scottie Pippen durante una serie de playoffs en 1994 contra los Knicks.</p><p>“Con cerveza rociada en mi cabeza en el Madison Square Garden”, dijo Lozano sobre la celebración de los fanáticos de los Knicks después de la victoria en el Juego 5. “No teníamos un cabina; no estábamos a pie de cancha. Estábamos en un rincón… con palomitas y cerveza”.</p><p>Lozano se pasó a la televisión en 1995. WGBO se había convertido en una filial de Univision y había lanzado un departamento de noticias dirigido por Jackie Gallardo, quien buscaba un presentador principal de deportes. El momento no pudo ser mejor porque WIND acababa de despedir a Lozano debido a recortes de personal.</p><p>Pero la radio no se iría de su vida. En 2015, los Bears trasladaron sus transmisiones en español a la filial de Univision, WRTO, y Lozano estuvo al frente. En 2016, los Blackhawks comenzaron a transmitir sus partidos en la estación y Lozano también los llamó. En 2017, el Fire regresó a WRTO y Lozano también los comentó.</p><p>“En un momento del año, tal vez cuatro o cinco meses, no tendría un día libre”, contó Lozano. “Pero fue increíble cubrir todos esos deportes”.</p><p>Lozano fue víctima nuevamente de los recortes de personal en 2021 —Univision recortó todos los departamentos de deportes del país tras la pandemia— y nuevamente encontró rápidamente un nuevo hogar.</p><p>Telemundo había estado indagando sobre el interés de Lozano en mudarse desde hace un par de años. Después de ser despedido, Lozano llamó al entonces presidente de NBC 5/Telemundo Chicago (WSNS), David Doebler. Aún estaba interesado.</p><p>“Mi hermano dice, ‘Debes tener una herradura o un pie de conejo en el trasero’”, dijo Lozano. “Yo dije, ‘Sí. Obtienes la oportunidad, pero luego tienes que aprovecharla’”.</p><p>Y así lo ha hecho. Y a lo largo del camino, se ha convertido en un pilar de la comunidad hispana de Chicago.</p><p>“Él ha estado en las salas de la gente durante 31 años”, dijo Kevin Cross, presidente de NBC 5/Telemundo Chicago. “Eso construye una conexión que puedes ver cuando está en la calle. Esa es la clave cuando se trata de la televisión local: ¿Cómo te conectas con tu audiencia?”.</p><p>“Crecí en Pilsen y La Villita” dijo Lozano. “No puedes ser más mexicano que eso”.</p><h3>La cobertura de la Copa del Mundo de Telemundo Chicago</h3><p>Telemundo (WSNS canal 44) transmitirá 92 partidos en vivo. El equipo nacional de Telemundo Deportes contará con equipos en las 16 ciudades sede, además de programas de estudio en la Ciudad de México, Miami y Nueva York, que proporcionarán cobertura previa al partido, en el medio tiempo y posterior al juego.</p><p>El dúo de ancla-reportero de <b>Héctor Lozano</b> y <b>Raúl Delgado</b> y el equipo de “Noticiero Telemundo Chicago” mantendrán a los televidentes informados sobre los acontecimientos de la Copa del Mundo. Lozano también compartirá sus “100 Datos de Mundial”.</p><p><i>Traducido con una herramienta de inteligencia artificial (AI) y editado por </i><a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/la-voz" target="_blank" ><i>La Voz Chicago</i></a></p>

entries.title: Caleb Williams: I'm fine with wherever Bears build stadium
entries.summary: <p><a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/bears/2026/06/11/bears-qb-caleb-williams-packers-micah-parsons-fire-ice-top-100-funny-nfl-rivalry-green-bay" target="_blank" >Caleb Williams</a> isn’t about to state his choice for where the <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/bears" target="_blank" >Bears</a> should play their home games going forward.</p><p>The Bears quarterback said Thursday he doesn’t care whether the Bears play in Hammond, Indiana, Arlington Heights, Chicago — or anywhere else.</p><p>“I’m going to play wherever there’s 120 by 53⅓ [yards] and it’s marked up with white lines and two end zones,” he said. “I’m OK with whatever. Whatever decision they make is whatever decision they make. I just want some green and my teammates and coaches and another team out there. And fans.”</p><p>One week ago, the Bears’ board of directors voted to continue forward with their exploration of building in Hammond — which fell short of being an ironclad commitment to moving across state lines. Bears president/CEO Kevin Warren told Illinois lawmakers he looked forward to continued conversations with them, and Gov. JB Pritzker said he’d call a special legislative session if politicians gain momentum on finding a way to give the team a property tax break.</p><p>The Bears have said they consider Arlington Heights, and not Chicago, the only suitable choice in Cook County.</p><p></p><bsp-list-loadmore class="PageListH" data-module data-hide-authors="true" data-hide-categories="true" data-hide-dates="true" entries.title: Bears QB Caleb Williams tackles Packers star Micah Parsons' fire-and-ice comment
entries.summary: <p><a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/bears" target="_blank" >Bears</a> quarterback Caleb Williams heard what Micah Parsons had to say about him — not only the implication that Williams was the <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/bears/2026/06/10/packers-star-micah-parsons-picks-bears-qb-caleb-williams-as-nfls-best-player-but-sends-warning" target="_blank" >top player in the league</a>, but his boast that the Packers star would be the one to slow him down.</p><p>“He said he’s fire and I'm ice, so we’ll see which one holds over,” Williams said Friday.</p><p>Williams dismissed Parsons’ threat — “I’ve got something for the Iceman, for sure,” he said —as funny.</p><p>“Obviously, it’s good jokes,” he said. “We’re football players on opposite teams, so it’s a little rivalry. Nothing taken to heart.”</p><p>That said, Williams probably wouldn’t flatter a Packers player the same way. He was asked if he’d ever vote for a rival as the top player in the NFL.</p><p>“Ummmm, probably not,” he said. “But that’s on my side of how I do things. But obviously, he’s a phenomenal player. You worry about him every single snap. So, kudos to him — and a speedy recovery [from his knee injury.]”</p><p></p><bsp-list-loadmore class="PageListH" data-module data-hide-authors="true" data-hide-categories="true" data-hide-dates="true" entries.title: Disability rights advocates file lawsuit over Illinois' 'dangerous' right-to-die law
entries.summary: <p>Disability rights and patient advocacy groups in Illinois have filed a federal lawsuit challenging a new law that allows terminally ill patients to seek medication to end their own lives.</p><p>The advocates oppose the <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/springfield/2025/11/03/illinois-right-to-die-bill-pritzker?_gl=1*k0oe2x*_up*MQ..*_ga*MTQxOTYyMDczNC4xNzgxMTk0MDEw*_ga_K0F0MB46T8*czE3ODExOTQwMDkkbzEkZzAkdDE3ODExOTQwMDkkajYwJGwwJGgw" target="_blank" >right-to-die legislation</a>, which will take effect in September. <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/politics/2025/12/12/illinois-right-to-die-pritzker-signs-law" target="_blank" >Gov. JB Pritzker signed the bill</a> into law last year, making Illinois the 12th state to permit medical aid in dying. The law allows certain terminally ill adults to obtain a prescription from a physician for medication they may choose to take to end their lives.</p><p>The suits, filed in Illinois and New York on Thursday, contend the legislation “discriminates against people with disabilities by singling them out for lethal prescriptions rather than providing equal access to the care, support, and suicide prevention services offered to those perceived as non or less disabled,” according to the End Assisted Suicide coalition.</p><p>“Assisted suicide laws in New York and Illinois create a separate and unequal system in which people with life-threatening disabilities are offered death instead of the support programs everyone else gets,” said Matt Vallière, president and executive director of plaintiff organization Institute for Patients' Rights.</p><p>“These legal actions are about affirming that every person has inestimable value and dignity, regardless of age, disability, or prognosis, and ensuring that no one is treated as disposable under the law.”</p><div class="Enhancement" data-align-center> <div class="Enhancement-item" data-crop=""> <figure class="Figure"><a class="Figure-content"><figcaption class="Figure-caption"><p>Ebony Payne, who is quadriplegic and from the South Side, is a plaintiff in a lawsuit challenging Illinois’ right-to-die legislation. </p></figcaption><span class="line"></span><div class="Figure-credit"><p>Provided by the End Assisted Suicide coalition</p></div></div> </figure> </div> </div><p>Under <a class="Link" href="https://ilga.gov/Legislation/BillStatus/FullText?GAID=18&DocNum=1950&DocTypeID=SB&LegId=161335&SessionID=114" target="_blank" >the law</a>, people 18 or older will be able to request a fatal medication if they’ve been diagnosed by two physicians with an illness that will result in death within six months.</p><p>Patients will have to make a series of oral and written requests themselves — not through a guardian, surrogate, advance legal document or other proxy — with witnesses attesting.</p><p>Physicians will have to confirm the patient is “of sound mind,” and inform them of other end-of-life options such as hospice and palliative care.</p><p>If prescribed a life-ending drug, patients would administer it themselves. Health care providers aren’t required to participate.</p><p>However, advocates claim the law violates the Americans with Disabilities Act, Section 504 of the Rehabilitation Act, and the Fourteenth Amendment’s due process and equal protection clauses, as well as state constitutional protections.</p><p>Advocates called the law “dangerous,” arguing it allows assisted suicide at a time when many people with disabilities are struggling to access support services. They pointed to ongoing Medicaid cuts, a nationwide shortage of home care workers and increasing pressures toward institutionalization, which they say have left many people with disabilities without the resources needed to live safely and independently.</p><p>Plaintiffs in Illinois include Chicago ADAPT, Progress Center for Independent Living, Dr. Nooshig Luz Salvador, Ebony Payne and Pam Heavens.</p><p>“I joined the lawsuit because of personal experiences that brought me really close to death and the people who I leaned on to do the right thing became the people to do the opposite,” Payne, a quadriplegic from Chicago, said in a statement. “It [the Illinois law] is a train wreck and is not what you expect from people who are obligated to do no harm.”</p>

entries.title: Tornado watch issued in Chicago area ahead of severe storms
entries.summary: <p>Weather officials issued a tornado watch for the Chicago area Thursday as severe storms are expected to move through the region.</p><p>The tornado watch is in effect until 9 p.m., according to the National Weather Service. Tornadoes, hail and wind gusts up to 80 mph are possible in the Chicago area and northwest Indiana.</p><p>A flood watch is also in effect until 11 p.m., weather officials said. Multiple rounds of heavy showers and thunderstorms are possible in the afternoon and evening, with rain rates up to 1 to 3 inches per hour.</p><p>The warning was issued a day after heavy rainfall and damaging winds swept through the area, causing widespread power outages and downed trees. About an inch of rain fell throughout the area <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/weather/2026/06/11/obstruction-on-tracks-causes-service-disruption-on-cta-yellow-line-trains-after-storms" target="_blank" ><u>Wednesday afternoon</u></a> with wind speeds reaching over 70 mph, weather officials said.</p>

entries.title: A double play? Really? Cubs manager Craig Counsell ejected after ‘umpires cost you two outs’
entries.summary: <p>DENVER — <b>Nico Hoerner</b> didn’t move from first base because <b>Moises Ballesteros</b> hit a foul ball.</p><p>That seemed to be what the players on the field thought. And that’s what the replay showed, a foul ball going off Ballesteros’ foot.</p><p>But in the sixth inning of <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/cubs/2026/06/11/cubs-seiya-suzuki-grand-slam-craig-counsell-power-numbers-home-runs-alex-bregman-nico-hoerner" >the Cubs’ 9-3 win over the Rockies</a> on Thursday, the foul ball ended up with the Cubs hitting into a double play.</p><p>The Rockies picked the ball up and threw to second, then first, as no one moved. The umpires called a pair of outs, and the Cubs went from a nascent scoring chance to down to their last out of the inning in a blink.</p><p>That didn’t sit well with manager <b>Craig Counsell</b>, who came out to voice his discontent. The umpires huddled up, but there was no change in the outcome of play, which was not reviewable, preventing Counsell from issuing a challenge.</p><p>After the double play stood, Counsell was angered further, letting the umpires know and eventually earning his second ejection of the season, much to the delight of both the Cubs and Rockies fans in attendance.</p><div class="Enhancement" data-align-center><div class="Enhancement-item"> <div class="ExternalContent-wrapper" > <div class="TweetUrl"> <blockquote class="twitter-tweet"><p lang="en" dir="ltr">Craig Counsell was ejected after the Rockies turned a double play on a clear foul ball. <a href="https://t.co/5Klsyn5Hul">pic.twitter.com/5Klsyn5Hul</a></p>— Foul Territory (@FoulTerritoryTV) <a href="https://x.com/FoulTerritoryTV/status/2065189279345824218?ref_src=twsrc%5Etfw">June 11, 2026</a></blockquote> <script async src="https://platform.x.com/widgets.js" charset="utf-8"></script> </div> </div> </div></div><p>“When umpires cost you two outs, that’s a big deal. That’s an inning, an inning over,” Counsell said after the game. “They didn’t see it. I don’t think you ever really see some of those plays. Like a hit by pitch, you don’t necessarily see it.</p><p>“But when the player reaction on the field — every player’s reaction on the field — is very obvious, that’s what they go on in those situations. I thought player reaction on the field was very obvious, and I was shocked when they got together that they didn’t think it was.”</p><p>The play ended up meaning little in the grand scheme of things. The Cubs held a 6-2 at the time and went on to win by six runs.</p><p>But that didn’t make it any less bizarre — or any less important to Counsell and the Cubs — in the moment.</p><h3><b>Cabrera bounces back</b></h3><p>The Cubs haven’t seen the version of <b>Edward Cabrera</b> they thought they traded for last offseason.</p><p>The right-handed pitcher turned in a 3.53 ERA with the Marlins a season ago, and the Cubs surrendered top prospect <b>Owen Caissie</b> in the belief that Cabrera could be a top-of-the-rotation arm for years to come.</p><p>The performance from Cabrera hasn’t matched that expectation yet. But Thursday, he did bounce back from a brutal start last time out, when he gave up eight runs and three homers in his return from a stay on the injured list.</p><p>This time, Cabrera held the Rockies to just two runs, the first time since his second start of the season April 5 in which he allowed fewer than three runs in an outing.</p><p>Those two runs did come on a pair of solo homers, and the Cubs’ worst-in-baseball total in that department is up to 102.</p><p>But it still qualified as a step forward for Cabrera as he and the Cubs seek the sort of contributions that can dramatically boost the injury-plagued rotation.</p><p>“This is obviously a tough place to pitch, and he was really effective today,” Counsell said. “It was a good bounce back to give him some confidence moving forward.</p><p>“He had some situations where I thought he lost it a little bit — just a very little bit, just five or six pitches — then came back and made some really good pitches. That’s part of pitching, and that’s part of having a good start.”</p><p></p><bsp-listcarousel class="PageListE" data-module data-column-count=3 data-hide-authors="true" data-hide-categories="true" entries.title: Mayor Johnson will ask City Council committee to repeal video gambling in Chicago
entries.summary: <p>The decision to lift the Chicago ban on video gambling terminals has divided the City Council and exacerbated tensions between alderpersons and Mayor Brandon Johnson.</p><p>On Thursday, a new and potentially broader front opened in the ongoing battle.</p><p>Johnson asked the City Council’s Committee on Workforce Development to meet Monday to consider direct introduction of an ordinance that would “authorize one or more agreements with the casino developer to enhance casino workforce capability to disallow video gaming terminals.”</p><p>“There’s some aldermen who are concerned about what this would mean for Bally’s operations in the city of Chicago, and their commitments to the city,” Workforce Development Chair Mike Rodriguez (22nd) told the Sun-Times. “This ordinance, if passed as it is," would repeal video gambling citywide and “start a conversation about revenue.”</p><p>Pressed on whether Johnson has the votes for a citywide repeal, Rodriguez said, “They’re whipping it,” the legislative term for attempting to round up the votes.</p><p>“There’ll be discussions over the weekend and on Monday in the committee, and we’ll see where folks are at. I hear smart people... and friends in labor, saying that Bally’s may balk on their millions that’s guaranteed to the city. That’s why we’re gonna have a conversation,” he said.</p><p>The $16.6 billion, 2026 budget <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/city-hall/2025/12/23/mayor-brandon-johnson-city-council-alternate-budget" target="_blank" >approved by a City Council </a>majority lifted the Chicago ban on video gambling and assumed that Chicago would generate $6.8 million by licensing newly legalized <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/city-hall/2025/09/16/video-gaming-in-chicago-proposal-anthony-beale-brandon-johnson" target="_blank" >video gambling terminals</a> across the city.</p><p>That’s based on the assumption that 80% of the 3,300 eligible establishments with off-premise liquor licenses will apply, but that the Illinois Gaming Board would take six to eight months to grant those licenses.</p><p>Johnson has raised strong objections to legalizing video gambling, in part because he believes it would violate the city’s host agreement with Bally’s, the gaming giant operating a temporary casino at Medinah Temple while building a permanent casino entertainment complex in River West.</p><p>The mayor’s City Council allies have either banned or attempted to ban video gambling terminals in their individual wards while buying time for Johnson to find the votes to repeal the ordinance citywide.</p><p>Ald. Anthony Beale (9th), City Council champion for lifting the Chicago ban, has been determined to maximize revenue from<a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/city-hall/2025/09/16/video-gaming-in-chicago-proposal-anthony-beale-brandon-johnson" target="_blank" > video gambling terminals</a> and eliminate competition for them, and has been trying to ban sweepstakes machines over Johnson’s objections.</p><p>On Thursday, Beale accused the mayor of introducing his proposed citywide repeal to the Workforce Development Committee chaired by his ally Rodriguez when it belongs in the License Committee.</p><p>“You can’t pass something in one committee and repeal it in another,” Beale said. “It’s just pathetic the games this administration plays.”</p><p>Beale has been warning for months that the mayor was working behind the scenes to round up enough votes to repeal the ordinance authorizing video gambling terminals at restaurants, bars and bowling alleys. He predicted Thursday that the mayor would fall short of the 26 votes he needs to reverse a fundamental element of the alternative budget.</p><p>“We had 31 aldermen to approve this along with the budget. I would be hard-pressed to believe he can get several aldermen change their position on this in order to try to repeal it. Are these people willing to blow a larger hole in the budget and go down the road with this administration, which has already shown they don’t have the capacity to run this city?”</p><p>License Committee Chair Debra Silverstein (50th), who voted with the City Council majority, is trying to protect her turf.</p><p>“Your decision to bypass the committee with clear jurisdiction and instead send this legislation to a committee perceived to be more politically favorable to you is a transparent attempt to avoid scrutiny and deliberation that should accompany any proposal of this magnitude,” Silverstein wrote in a letter to Johnson.</p><p>“Unfortunately, this action is consistent with a broader pattern of efforts by your administration to circumvent the legislative powers of the City Council when doing so is politically expedient.”</p><p>The mayor’s office had no immediate comment on Silverstein’s letter, or the attempt to repeal video gambling in Chicago.</p><p>Bally’s has warned repeatedly that lifting Chicago<a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/city-hall/2025/09/16/video-gaming-in-chicago-proposal-anthony-beale-brandon-johnson" target="_blank" > ban on video gambling </a>would cost the cash-strapped city $74 million in annual revenue and as many as 1,050 jobs at its temporary and permanent casinos.</p><p>The casino giant has further warned that lifting the long-standing Chicago ban would force the Johnson administration to renegotiate “critical elements” of its host agreement, wipe out a yearly $4 million lump-sum payment from Bally’s and shrink the jackpot needed to save police and fire pension funds.</p>

entries.title: Seiya Suzuki backs Cubs’ confidence in turnaround with sweep-avoiding slam as power bats finally show up
entries.summary: <p>DENVER — It’s too early to say whether Seiya Suzuki slammed the <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/cubs" >Cubs</a> out of their early-summer freefall.</p><p>But boy, did this team need a hit like that one.</p><p>The team’s struggles with runners in scoring position have received plenty of attention during what’s become a monthlong losing stretch, but its lack of power has been just as glaring.</p><p>Though they got a solo homer in each of the first two games of their series in mile-high Colorado, the typically hitter-friendly conditions did little to goose the Cubs’ sputtering bats.</p><p>Until the fourth inning Thursday, that is, when Suzuki came through with the knock his team has so frequently failed to deliver over the past several weeks, sending a grand slam out to left field to flip a 1-0 deficit into a 4-1 lead.</p><div class="Enhancement" data-align-center><div class="Enhancement-item"> <div class="ExternalContent-wrapper" > <div class="TweetUrl"> <blockquote class="twitter-tweet"><p lang="en" dir="ltr">Seiya Suzuki's 10th homer of the season is GRAND ‼️ <a href="https://t.co/2QLwOtN6PN">pic.twitter.com/2QLwOtN6PN</a></p>— MLB (@MLB) <a href="https://x.com/MLB/status/2065163410103300545?ref_src=twsrc%5Etfw">June 11, 2026</a></blockquote> <script async src="https://platform.x.com/widgets.js" charset="utf-8"></script> </div> </div> </div></div><p>The Cubs rode onto a 9-3 win — one that also featured Alex Bregman and Carson Kelly leaving the yard in the team’s first three-homer game since late April — to avoid being swept by the Rockies.</p><p>“As a team, in those opportunities, we haven’t gotten that one hit,” Suzuki said through an interpreter. “Today, we can use that as a breakthrough.”</p><p>Only a couple hours earlier, manager Craig Counsell lamented his team’s lack of power. Coming into Thursday, the Cubs owned a .332 slugging percentage that ranked as baseball’s lowest since May 9, the day after they completed the second of their two 10-game win streaks this season.</p><p>Suzuki’s slam and some long-awaited pop from the team’s big free-agent addition served as a nice remedy.</p><p>But will it be more than just a temporary one?</p><p>Just recently, the Cubs experienced some false monkey-off-their-backs moments with walk-off wins at Wrigley Field that preceded more losing.</p><p>Inside a victorious postgame locker room Thursday, no one was ready to claim this win as a season-saver.</p><p>“We have maybe three guys playing to their potential. So we’ve got a lot of work to do, and we’ve got to be better,” Bregman said. “We’re way better of a ballclub than we’ve shown. We’ve got to look in the mirror and figure out a way to get it done on the field.</p><p>“We’ve got to play better. Today was a good step in the right direction.”</p><p>Even if one win doesn’t start a turnaround, the Cubs remain confident one is coming eventually.</p><p>Why? With this roster, they believe it has to.</p><p>“We have very good offensive players. They’ve shown that this year,” Counsell said before the game. “The length [of the losing stretch], yeah, it’s surprising, absolutely. And it’s challenging. We’re all trying to do our best to put it in the right direction. We haven’t been able to come up with solutions so far.</p><p>“We have very talented, good players, and that absolutely creates optimism.”</p><p>The “it’s a long season” argument doesn’t sit well with frustrated fans who want improved results and want them now. But there is plenty of time left in baseball’s marathon for the Cubs to get back on track.</p><p>Losing in May and June hasn’t changed this team’s expectations for what they’ll be doing in October.</p><p>The problem, as has been the case in recent years, is that getting back on track doesn’t necessarily mean catching the Brewers. The Cubs woke up in the Mile High City a seeming mile from first place Thursday, eight games back after falling to .500 the night before.</p><p>Baseball’s expanded postseason means the Cubs’ playoff and championship dreams are in no way dashed, should they make the turnaround they believe they can.</p><p>But will the Brewers let them back in the division race? Or will it be “wild card or bust” for a team that was thinking “World Series or bust” a month ago?</p><p>“We’ve got a lot of very established players that have done great things in this league,” second baseman Nico Hoerner told the Sun-Times, “but the game doesn’t care about that. It’s all about the next pitch and what you’re onto next.</p><p>“I don’t think the confidence in our group has changed at all.”</p><p></p><p></p><bsp-listcarousel class="PageListE" data-module entries.title: Caitlin Clark holds two truths about her competitive fire. Can we?
entries.summary: <p>INDIANAPOLIS — Watch Fever star Caitlin Clark play for 10 minutes and you'll have an opinion on the way she moves.</p><p>She taunts opponents after a big shot. She yells at her coaches and officials. She prances around like a stadium MC after a scoring run. She postures like she's ready to throw down in a heated moment — then walks away and lets her teammates handle it.</p><p>Love it or hate it, you can't ignore it. You have to have an opinion because she's basketball's biggest star.</p><p>So here's an opinion: One thing I've always liked about Clark is her bravado. She's full of herself, unafraid of consequence, in ways women are typically taught not to be. She's launching that 30-footer whether her coach called it or not.</p><p>I wish I'd had more of that as a player, and I wish I had more of it in my life now.</p><p>Here's another opinion: I sometimes find her outbursts unsettling. They can come off like entitlement from a straight white woman in a league built by — and precious to — so many who are Black, queer and otherwise marginalized. Plus, her "fans" often defend her by diminishing the league's history and its players, which makes me feel protective.</p><p>I acknowledge this reaction isn't fair to Clark. From my point of view as a <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/chicago-sky" target="_blank" >Sky</a> beat reporter, I don't know what's going on underneath the surface. I don't know whether she feels entitled — or just frustrated, pressured, or something else. I don't know what she really thinks of the obnoxious fans-slash-trolls, or whether she feels responsible for them.</p><p>I do know she's a great player — the league’s leader in assists — whose teammates all speak highly of her.</p><div class="Enhancement" data-align-center><div class="Enhancement-item"> <div class="ExternalContent-wrapper" data-embed> <iframe width="200" height="113" src="https://www.youtube.com/embed/CsLwE4GbjlM?feature=oembed" frameborder="0" allow="accelerometer; autoplay; clipboard-write; encrypted-media; gyroscope; picture-in-picture; web-share" referrerpolicy="strict-origin-when-cross-origin" allowfullscreen title="CAITLIN CLARK CALLS GAME 🤯 CC hits dagger to seal Fever's victory over the Mystics 💪 | WNBA on ESPN"></iframe> </div> </div></div><p>So here's one more opinion, maybe a fairer one: I'm interested in her thoughts on the connection between competitiveness, body language and greatness. Columnist Candace Buckner recently asked her about her body language, and her answer got me thinking.</p><p>"I think it's something I can always work on," she said. "You go back, you look at the mirror, and I'm competitive and I have an edge, and I think at the same time it's what makes me great. But it's not something you always love, too.</p><p>"I think that competitive fire and that drive and that passion, that joy and that edge, that's what people come to watch. That's what they love. It's not always going to be pretty — and look at some of the best players in the world or some of the best players who have ever played this game, and they're fierce. They're fiery. They're competitive."</p><p>I hear her holding two things at once: that her fire is essential, and that it's "not something you always love." Which speaks to an interesting tension in our understanding of greatness.</p><p>There's the conventional, masculine model: Greatness comes from drive and dominance, all stemming from an uncontrollable impulse to win. Michael Jordan punched a teammate. Kobe Bryant bowled one over.</p><p>But there's an alternative understanding, too: that the same competitive impulse can turn into perfectionism, rumination and fear of failure — the very things that pull an athlete out of flow.</p><p>It's part of why so many great ones turn to meditation, a fundamentally uncompetitive practice. It's about staying in the moment. Detaching from outcome. Which, ironically, tends to produce better results.</p><p>Lately I've been asking myself: What is the connection between my need to win and my own potential for greatness?</p><p>In my work as a journalist, my competitiveness can make my coverage deeper and more compelling. But it can also cause me to rush, to forget to hydrate, to forget to be vulnerable — all of which work against my writing.</p><p>I first started thinking about my own competitiveness as a basketball player, and what I realized was that I wasn't just driven by a desire to win. I was driven by a desire to be loved — to not let down my dad, who taught me the game and could be harsh in his criticism.</p><p>I also realized that, as a form of protection from the car rides home, I became ultra-critical of myself.</p><p>I did a lot of work in adulthood to reach those realizations, and guess what: I'm still super critical of myself!</p><p>I'll be working to meet my deadline and suddenly feel a tension in my neck, notice an inner commentary about everything I’m doing wrong, and think: Wow, I am putting so much pressure on myself right now.</p><p>That isn't something that's ever going away. It's just something I can try to notice and, like Clark often says, try to channel more positively.</p><p>She may be doing that with her body language this season. Though the buzz about her is that she's yelling at officials more, she's made progress in another area: She's no longer visibly upset when teammates botch her passes.</p><p>Maybe the redirect of her competitive ire from teammates to officials isn't the perfect or prettiest evolution.</p><p>But my last opinion is this: change is hard, and slow, and nonlinear. We should acknowledge small improvements, even if they don't look how we imagined them. </p>

entries.title: White Sox' game vs. Braves delayed by approaching storms
entries.summary: <p>The White Sox' game Thursday night against the Braves is being delayed by a line of approaching storms set to descend on Rate Field, the team announced. First pitch initially was scheduled for 6:40 p.m.</p><p>Left-hander Anthony Kay (5-1, 4.40 ERA) is scheduled to face former Sox lefty Martin Perez (4-3, 3.02). The Sox have taken the first two games in the three-game series against the Braves, who have the best record in baseball.</p><p>The Sox are in first place in the American League Central by a half-game over the idle Guardians, who were just swept by the Yankees.<br></p>

entries.title: Mayor’s choice for human relations chief uses confirmation hearing to recall first exposure to hate crime
entries.summary: <p>Kenneth Gunn got his first taste of a Chicago hate crime as a kid growing up in racially changing Englewood attending an elementary school “on the white side” of the neighborhood.</p><p>Gunn lived on the “the Black side" of Ashland Avenue. He and his brother were allowed to go to Earle Elementary School on the west side of Ashland, but were warned to “come straight home right after school or you might run into a little trouble.”</p><p>Gunn’s older brother ignored the warning and was “beaten by the neighborhood bullies," he told the City Council’s Committee on Health and Human Relations at his confirmation hearing Thursday. </p><p>The Gunn brothers were then transferred to an all-Black school on the east side of Ashland Avenue for their 7th and 8th grade years after parents who feared the West Side was “becoming too Black” demanded a boundary change.</p><p>"That was my first introduction to hate crimes," Gunn said Thursday. “It hurt like hell to leave my friends, just like it did when my white friends moved away a few years earlier."</p><p>On Thursday, Gunn relived that bitter memory and promised to bring the sensitivity he gained from that experience to what is slated to be his new job as <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/2026/06/02/johnsons-choice-to-lead-human-relations-commission-vows-to-improve-frayed-relationship-with-jewish-leaders" >head of Chicago’s Commission on Human Relations.</a></p><p>The Health and Human Relations Committee confirmed his appointment with only one dissenting vote, setting the stage for final City Council approval on Wednesday.</p><div href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/city-hall/2026/03/25/human-relations-commissioner-nancy-andrade-resignation-antisemitism-report" >who resigned in March </a>to protest what critics contend was Johnson’s attempt to whitewash a long-awaited report that was supposed to focus solely on antisemitism.</p><p>Last month, Johnson unveiled a strategy to combat hate crimes that Jewish leaders condemned as an insensitive and inadequate response to the surge in anti-Jewish hate crimes.</p><p>Johnson’s plan called for creating a “Jewish Engagement Council to serve as a direct bridge for dialogue” between residents, community leaders and the mayor’s office, and an “Interconnected Chicago Council” to address “fragmentation between communities.”</p><p>The commission-approved version that prompted Andrade’s resignation was triggered by a 58% rise in reported anti-Jewish hate crimes from 2023 to 2024.</p><p>It recommended a task force to combat anti-Jewish hate, mandatory training on antisemitism for city employees, teachers and students in the Chicago Public Schools, and a dedicated unit within the Chicago Police Department specifically trained to combat hate crimes.</p><p>Although Jews were “most heavily impacted” by hate crimes committed in 2024, Gunn favors the mayor’s version of the report because of its flexibility and the “broader spectrum” it applies to “how we respond to hate.”</p><p>“It’s not just Jewish voices saying, this is happening and we have to address it. You have all these people around you to help do it. You can get the best of the best to address these," Gunn said.</p><p>Ald. Ray Lopez (15th) accused Gunn of acquiescing to the Johnson administration’s effort to “dilute the impact of Jewish hate that’s running rabid in this city and in government, while also trying to elevate numbers to a level of questionable comparison." </p><p>“I find that to be a false equivalence... to say that something that is in the single digits should be looked at and viewed from the same lens when we know that particular community has been completely ostracized, demonized from this building and beyond," he said.</p><p><a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/real-estate/2026/05/15/edgewater-synagogue-emanuel-updated-project-plans-3-lakefront-towers" target="_blank" ></a></p><p></p><p></p><p></p><p>South Side Ald. Lamont Robinson (4th), who chairs the City Council’s LGBTQ Caucus, urged Gunn to focus on the “high rates of hate crimes to our trans brothers and sisters, particularly those that are African-American.”</p><p>“I’m curious to know how your office can work to figure out how we can set the example in the country of solving a lot of the murders that go unsolved. How do we educate the community?” Robinson said. "How can I educate my colleagues [who] still don’t understand... there are LGBTQ+ folk in all 77 neighborhoods?"</p>

entries.title: Spiking gas prices spur some Chicagoans to stop looking, amid rising food prices and inflation
entries.summary: <p>Alejandro Vasquez was filling up his Toyota Prius Thursday morning at one of the priciest gas stations in Chicago.</p><p>The Shell station at 130 W. North Ave. in Old Town was selling regular gas at $5.80 a gallon, one of the highest prices for a gallon of gas in the city, according to data from GasBuddy.</p><p>But after months of climbing gas prices, Vasquez, who earns extra cash delivering groceries, and other drivers interviewed on Thursday said they are now resigned to the steep prices.</p><p>“My friend and I talked about this,” Vasquez, 29, said. “We treat it kind of like a phone bill, though. I don't even look at it. What else am I gonna do?”</p><p>As summer begins, consumers are finding no relief from climbing gas and food prices. Just a <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/economy/2026/03/04/chicagoans-uneasy-gas-prices-iran-war-straight-hormuz-supply-chain-disruptions" >few months ago</a>, the average price for a gallon of regular gas in the Chicago metro area was around $4, according to GasBuddy. As of Thursday, the average price was $4.52. The Chicago metro area's record-high gas price was in 2022 when it reached $6.07, largely due to the war in Ukraine.</p><p>Vasquez said he stopped at the station because he was "literally out of gas.” </p><p>“It is funny when you notice [gas prices]. I think when they get more predatory is it's in places where there's no gas stations. So they know that you're stopping because you have to,” he said.</p><p>A nearby BP station, at 1647 N. La Salle Dr., was also priced at $5.80 for a gallon of regular gas. The two stations in Old Town are right off Lake Shore Drive, easily catching drivers when they're in need.</p><p>GasBuddy data showed only one station in Chicago had a higher price — a Marathon near Fulton Market, where the price was $6 this week.</p><p>“Oh Lord, there’s nothing else to say about gas prices,” Reggie Russell, 40, said at the BP station. </p><p>Russell, an Uber driver, normally travels to Indiana to get cheaper gas. Prices there Thursday were an average of $3.38, according to GasBuddy.</p><p>“It doesn’t matter where in Indiana you go; as long as you go to Indiana it’s good,” he said.</p><p>It used to take about $20 to fill up his Dodge Caravan, but now it’s double that, he said.</p><p>After filling up Thursday, he was headed for his first Uber pickup of the day.</p><p>For Lia Montelongo, 51, fueling up her 2020 Jeep isn’t going to make her lose sleep.</p><p>“I really don’t care about the gas prices,” the Equinox fitness instructor, model and actress said. “I notice the higher prices, but I don’t care. I have to drive so it’s like I’ve got to just suit up and show up.”</p><p>She lives in Mokena, a southwest suburb, and fills up a couple times a week.</p><p>“The only reason why I do stop here is because it's on my way to get home,” she said. “It's like I know I'm safe. I'm gonna jump on the Lake Shore Drive and go home.”</p><div class="Enhancement" data-align-center> <div class="Enhancement-item" data-crop=""> <figure class="Figure"><a class="AnchorLink"
